title: Computer Is Slow
cardText: Diagnose a Windows computer that has become slow or unresponsive.
Investigate high CPU, memory and disk usage, startup programs, updates, malware and storage health.
Identify software bottlenecks and hardware limitations before recommending upgrades.
text: This guide helps diagnose slow performance on Windows computers.
Identify whether the slowdown affects the entire computer or only specific applications.
Check recent changes, Task Manager resource usage, storage health and background activity.
Investigate Windows updates, startup programs, malware and thermal throttling where relevant.
Use the diagnostic results to determine whether software repairs or hardware upgrades are appropriate.

identifyScope.title: Identify the performance problem
body: Determine whether the entire computer is slow or the problem affects only one application.
Check whether Windows itself is slow to respond, applications take unusually long to open or file operations are delayed.
If only one application is affected, investigate that application before making system-wide changes.
If the entire computer is slow, continue with the system performance checks.

checkSingleApp.title: Investigate the slow application
body: Check the application's CPU, memory and disk usage in Task Manager.
Check for available application updates and known compatibility issues.
Test whether the application behaves normally after restarting it.
If appropriate, disable unnecessary extensions or plugins.
Use the application's repair or reinstall option if its files or configuration appear damaged.
If performance remains poor, determine whether it depends on an external network service.

checkAppNetworkDependency.title: Check application network dependencies
body: Determine whether the application relies on internet access, cloud storage, a database or a remote server.
Compare its performance with local applications such as Notepad or File Explorer.
Check for delays when accessing network shares or cloud-synchronised folders.
If local applications perform normally, investigate the relevant network connection, VPN, server or cloud service.
If local applications are also slow, continue with whole-system diagnostics.

networkRelatedAppIssue.title: Network or application service bottleneck likely
body: The slowdown appears limited to an application that depends on an external service.
Check network latency, DNS, VPN connections and server availability as appropriate.
For shared applications or files, test access from another computer.
Check the service provider's status information if a cloud application is affected.
Avoid unnecessary Windows repairs until the external dependency has been investigated.

recentOrLongTerm.title: Identify when performance deteriorated
body: Determine whether the computer became slow recently or has been consistently slow over time.
A recent slowdown may coincide with updates, new applications, malware or hardware deterioration.
Long-standing poor performance may result from limited RAM, a mechanical hard drive or insufficient processing capacity.
Choose the relevant branch to narrow down the likely cause.

checkRecentChanges.title: Check recent system changes
body: Review recently installed applications, Windows updates, drivers and browser extensions.
Check whether a new antivirus, backup utility or cloud synchronisation application was installed.
Compare the timing of any changes with when performance deteriorated.
If a relevant change is identified, test reversing it before proceeding with broader troubleshooting.

link.name: Microsoft: Improve Windows performance
link.description: Official guidance covering updates, applications, background activity and performance problems.

undoRecentChange.title: Reverse the suspected change
body: Temporarily disable, uninstall or roll back the change associated with the slowdown.
For driver updates, use the manufacturer's recommended rollback procedure.
For recently installed applications, check whether they added background services or startup processes.
Make one change at a time and compare performance afterwards.
If the computer remains slow, continue investigating storage and resource usage.

checkHardwareAge.title: Assess hardware performance limitations
body: Check the processor model, installed RAM and whether Windows runs from an HDD or SSD.
Use Task Manager, Performance to view installed memory, processor details and disk type.
Older processors, limited RAM and mechanical hard drives can significantly affect Windows responsiveness.
However, hardware age alone does not prove that an upgrade is necessary.
Determine whether the system is consistently limited by its hardware or whether another performance fault is present.

link.name: Microsoft: Signs that a PC may need upgrading
link.description: Official guidance for assessing ageing or insufficient computer hardware.

hardwareUpgradeLikely.title: Assess potential hardware upgrades
body: Check which hardware component is limiting performance.
Replacing a mechanical system drive with an SSD often significantly improves startup and application loading times.
Increasing RAM can help when memory pressure causes excessive paging to disk.
A processor upgrade may be impractical on older systems.
Check compatibility, upgrade costs and current Windows support before proceeding.
If the limitation is uncertain, continue with storage and Task Manager diagnostics before purchasing hardware.

hardwareUpgradeRecommendation.title: Hardware upgrade recommended
body: The system's performance limitation has been identified.
Choose an SSD upgrade when mechanical disk performance is the main bottleneck.
Increase RAM when available memory is consistently insufficient.
Confirm motherboard, memory and storage compatibility before purchasing components.
Back up data before replacing the system drive.
Compare the cost of upgrading with replacing the computer, particularly if it cannot support a current operating system.

checkDiskSpace.title: Check available system drive space
body: Open Settings, System, Storage.
Check the free space available on the Windows system drive.
Low free space can interfere with Windows updates, temporary files and virtual memory.
As a practical guideline, maintaining approximately 15 to 20 percent free space may help, although the amount needed varies with drive size and workload.
If storage is critically low, remove unnecessary files before continuing.

link.name: Microsoft: Windows Storage settings
link.description: Official guidance for inspecting disk usage and managing available storage.

freeDiskSpace.title: Free system drive space
body: Open Settings, System, Storage.
Review Temporary files and Cleanup recommendations.
Remove unnecessary temporary files and unused applications.
Review Downloads and Recycle Bin contents before deleting anything.
Move large personal files to another suitable storage location if necessary.
Do not delete unknown files from Windows system directories.
Check whether sufficient space has been recovered and retest performance.

link.name: Microsoft: Manage storage with Storage Sense
link.description: Official instructions for safely removing temporary files and managing storage.

freeDiskSpace.alt: Windows 11 Storage settings showing temporary files and cleanup recommendations
freeDiskSpace.caption: Use Windows Storage settings to identify and remove unnecessary files.

openTaskManager.title: Analyse resource usage in Task Manager
body: Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager.
Select Processes and examine CPU, Memory, Disk and Network usage.
Sort by the relevant column to identify processes consuming the most resources.
Check whether high usage persists while the computer feels slow.
Brief spikes are normal; look for sustained activity that coincides with the performance problem.
Use the Performance tab to check total memory usage, processor load and disk activity.

link.name: ASUS: Use Task Manager to investigate performance
link.description: Manufacturer instructions showing Windows Task Manager resource monitoring.

link.name: Microsoft: Improve PC performance
link.description: Official guidance for identifying high-resource applications and background tasks.

openTaskManager.alt: Windows Task Manager Processes tab showing CPU, memory and disk usage by application
openTaskManager.caption: Sort processes by CPU, Memory or Disk to identify sustained resource usage.

identifyHighUsage.title: Identify the performance bottleneck
body: Determine which resource remains heavily utilised while the slowdown occurs.
High CPU usage may indicate an intensive or malfunctioning process.
High memory usage may cause excessive paging when insufficient RAM is available.
High disk activity may indicate storage delays, background tasks or a failing drive.
High network activity may indicate downloads, cloud synchronisation or remote-service delays.
Choose the branch corresponding to the main bottleneck.

cpuOrMemoryHigh.title: Investigate CPU or memory pressure
body: In Task Manager, identify the processes responsible for sustained CPU or memory usage.
Check whether the processes belong to known applications, Windows services or third-party utilities.
Compare memory usage with the total installed RAM.
If memory is nearly exhausted, check for unusually large application usage or excessive browser tabs.
Investigate processes you do not recognise before ending them.
Avoid terminating essential Windows system processes.

handleKnownHeavyProcess.title: Resolve excessive application resource usage
body: Check whether the identified process is performing an expected task.
Close or reconfigure applications using excessive resources unnecessarily.
For browsers, reduce tabs or investigate extensions.
For backup, antivirus, indexing or synchronisation tasks, check whether the workload can complete or be scheduled differently.
If an application consistently uses excessive resources, check for updates or known issues.
Retest performance after reducing the load.

scanForMalware.title: Check for malware or unwanted software
body: Open Windows Security, Virus & threat protection.
Run a scan using the installed, trusted antivirus product.
If the problem persists or suspicious behaviour is present, consider a full scan or Microsoft Defender Offline scan where supported.
Investigate unknown startup entries, suspicious browser extensions and unexpected background processes.
Avoid installing untrusted system cleaners or software claiming to fix every performance problem.
Review any detections before removing software.

link.name: Microsoft: Scan for malware with Windows Security
Microsoft: Improve PC performance
link.description: Includes guidance on malware-related performance problems.

removeThreats.title: Remove detected malware or unwanted software
body: Follow the trusted security application's instructions to quarantine or remove confirmed threats.
Restart the computer if required.
Run another scan to check whether the threat remains.
Check whether suspicious startup processes or browser modifications return.
If sensitive accounts may have been compromised, change affected passwords from a clean device.
If performance remains poor after cleanup, continue investigating background services and startup applications.

diskOrNetworkHigh.title: Investigate disk and network activity
body: Use Task Manager to identify processes responsible for sustained disk or network activity.
Check for Windows Update, antivirus scans, indexing, cloud synchronisation, backup software or large downloads.
On a mechanical HDD, sustained high disk active time may cause substantial delays even when transfer speeds appear low.
Check whether the activity corresponds to a legitimate background task.
If the activity is unexpected, investigate drive health and relevant system errors.

waitForBackgroundTask.title: Manage background activity
body: Identify the background process responsible for the load.
Allow legitimate updates, backup jobs or indexing tasks to complete when practical.
Consider rescheduling non-essential tasks that interfere with normal use.
Check cloud synchronisation software for repeated failures or unusually large queues.
After the activity settles, retest computer performance.
If the computer remains slow, investigate the drive.

checkDiskHealth.title: Check SSD or HDD health
body: Identify the system drive model and whether it is an HDD or SSD.
Use the drive manufacturer's diagnostic utility or another reputable tool to inspect SMART health information.
Check for media errors, critical warnings, repeated I/O errors or abnormal response times.
Review Windows Event Viewer for recurring disk or storage-controller errors.
Mechanical clicking noises, freezing during file access and SMART failure warnings are reasons to investigate urgently.
If drive failure is suspected, back up important data before running intensive tests.
Do not assume high disk usage alone proves the drive is defective.

backupAndReplaceDrive.title: Storage hardware fault identified
body: Storage diagnostics indicate that the system drive may be failing.
Back up important files immediately if they remain accessible.
Confirm the affected drive and its replacement compatibility.
Replace the drive if a hardware fault is established.
Restore the operating system and user data from an appropriate backup, or reinstall Windows.
If the drive contains valuable data and is severely failing, consider professional data recovery before further use.

checkStartupPrograms.title: Review Windows startup applications
body: Open Task Manager using Ctrl + Shift + Esc.
Select Startup apps.
Review enabled applications and their reported startup impact.
Look for unnecessary launchers, update utilities, chat clients and other applications that do not need to start automatically.
Disable only applications that are not required for normal operation.
Do not disable security software, essential hardware utilities or managed business software without understanding their purpose.

link.name: Microsoft: Configure Windows startup applications
link.description: Official instructions for managing startup apps through Settings and Task Manager.

disableStartupApps.title: Disable unnecessary startup applications
body: Disable non-essential startup applications in Task Manager.
Restart Windows and compare startup time and responsiveness.
Check whether disabled applications are still required for particular tasks.
Re-enable an application if disabling it causes an unexpected problem.
If performance remains poor, check Windows Update activity.

link.name: Microsoft: Manage startup apps
link.description: Official guidance for disabling and re-enabling Windows startup applications.

checkWindowsUpdates.title: Check Windows Update activity
body: Open Settings, Windows Update.
Check for updates that are downloading, installing, repeatedly failing or awaiting a restart.
Use Task Manager to determine whether update-related processes are consuming significant resources.
Large updates and background maintenance can temporarily affect performance.
Repeated installation failures or update loops may indicate a problem that requires separate troubleshooting.
Check update history when the slowdown began after a particular Windows update.

link.name: Microsoft: Windows performance troubleshooting
link.description: Official recommendations for Windows updates and system performance.

completeUpdates.title: Resolve update-related performance problems
body: Allow legitimate updates to complete where possible.
Restart Windows when an update requires it.
If updates repeatedly fail or remain stuck, use the Windows Update Failed troubleshooting guide.
Check whether update-related background load has returned to normal.
Retest overall system responsiveness after the update completes.

checkBrowserLoad.title: Check browser resource usage
body: Check whether slow performance mainly occurs when a browser is open.
Review browser memory and CPU usage in Task Manager.
Reduce unnecessary tabs and investigate extensions consuming excessive resources.
Test the browser without unnecessary extensions or using another browser.
If only websites are slow while local applications run normally, investigate internet connectivity or DNS separately.
Determine whether browser cleanup resolves the performance issue.

browserCleanup.title: Browser performance issue identified
body: The performance problem is associated with browser processes, extensions or excessive tab usage.
Remove or disable unnecessary extensions and close unused tabs.
Check for browser updates and restart the browser.
If performance problems affect only online content, investigate the internet connection and any browser-specific network settings.
Retest performance using the normal workload.

checkThermalThrottling.title: Check temperatures and thermal throttling
body: Use a reputable hardware monitoring utility to inspect CPU and GPU temperatures.
Check whether performance drops as temperatures increase during normal workloads.
Compare readings with the manufacturer's supported operating limits.
Look for thermal throttling, unusually low CPU clock speeds under load or cooling fans that are not operating properly.
Inspect ventilation and airflow restrictions.
Temperature limits vary by model, so avoid relying on a single universal threshold.

cleanCoolingSystem.title: Correct cooling and airflow problems
body: Shut down and disconnect power before cleaning accessible cooling components.
Remove dust from vents, filters and fans using an appropriate method.
Check that fans operate and heatsinks are mounted correctly.
For laptops, avoid blocking ventilation and follow manufacturer service instructions.
If thermal paste or cooler installation is suspected, inspect and service the cooling system as appropriate.
Recheck temperatures and performance after correcting the cooling issue.

checkUserProfile.title: Compare performance with another Windows profile
body: If available, sign in with another existing Windows user account.
Compare login time, File Explorer responsiveness and general desktop performance.
Check whether the slowdown is limited to the original profile.
Profile-specific problems can involve startup applications, cloud synchronisation, mapped drives or damaged user settings.
If both profiles are slow, continue with system-wide diagnostics.

profileIssueLikely.title: Windows user profile issue likely
body: Performance is significantly better using another Windows profile.
Investigate profile-specific startup processes, browser data, cloud synchronisation and mapped network drives.
Check for damaged user settings or unusually large profile folders.
Back up important user files and application configuration before creating a replacement profile.
If a new profile is required, migrate data carefully and verify that applications work correctly.

finalPerformanceAssessment.title: Further performance diagnostics required
body: The computer remains slow after checking resource usage, storage health, startup processes, updates, malware and temperatures.
Review Windows event logs for recurring hardware, storage or application errors.
Consider a clean boot to isolate non-Microsoft services and startup software.
Check installed RAM capacity and whether the system drive is causing excessive paging or disk delays.
Test memory and storage with suitable diagnostics if the symptoms justify it.
Consider an SSD or RAM upgrade when a genuine hardware bottleneck has been identified.
Back up important data before attempting major repairs or reinstalling Windows.
Compare the cost of further diagnosis and upgrades with replacement if the computer is significantly outdated.
